blocks.x: Being able to read Japanese literature is one of those skills that goes away (quickly) as time passes if you don’t keep reading. Use it or lose it. Since it had been a few months I decided to pick up a novel at the local Kinokuniya store in Beaverton. My requirements were three: not too long, a genre that I was into (some like murder mysteries I’ve grown bored of), and an interesting first page. “Novel” (小説) by Mado Nozaki (野崎まど) easily fit the bill so I picked it up.
I want to emphasize that this is a novel named “Novel”. Though a good or interesting title isn’t a huge thing for me, to be honest I really like this one. (And I really liked the cover too.)

With my literature reading skills being a little rusty (not to mention my usual too-many-hobbies problem), this read took around a month, and there were some days where I only got through a handful of pages. The slow speed is partially due to the story being slow at parts, though this is a vicious circle since I think the slower parts are harder to appreciate when you are reading slower.
“Novel” is one of those novels that could be ruined by giving out too much information, so I’m going to give some basic details and then get vague after that.

The story is about two boys who are both deeply into literature, to the point that they spend their days and nights reading, whenever they can. This is a nice setup, and surely fits the title. At some point they stumble upon a mysterious mansion where an old man lives, and they end up sneaking in and discovering all sorts of things there. I’ll just say that the old man seems to have some important connection to books, though the details are vague until later in the story.

I think my slow reading speed is partly at fault, but there were large portions of this book where I felt not much was going on, or should I say not much of great importance. It doesn’t help that right before starting this book I read someone say how Japanese books are typically very slow paced, where everything happens in the character’s minds. I only think this is true to an extent (speaking generally), but indeed it applies to a big part of this book.

The slow paced story is punctuated by dramatic scenes in a few places, but they were few and far between and I wish there was more. One of those scenes ended very oddly, to the point I had to read it two or three times to make sure I understood. Even now, that scene seems to end very oddly, basically ruining what was a really interesting idea. To be fair, after reading to the end things make a bit more sense, but still I think one of the developments was a bit awkward.

Some of the dramatic scenes involve dreamlike or fantasy-ish elements, which again are interesting, but the great contrast between these and the rest of the boring plot just frustrated me. In some ways it reminded me of one of those animes that seems normal, but has a super crazy plot twist at some point that has you scratching your head. I understand the idea of starting slow to build up to an exciting twist, but I felt like 60-80% of the book was slow and boring (in some ways this reminds of Haruki Murakami’s style, though back in the day I didn’t mind the slow pace as much). Had I, like the two main characters, loved novels more than anything else and had nothing else to do but read this book, perhaps I would have read late into the night and finished it quickly, and I guess the slowness wouldn’t have bothered me as much.

Japanese-wise the book is definitely “literary”, with a bunch of uncommon kanji and words that had me looking up things here and there. For the record, I don’t mind that at all, and it even helped inspire a personal project related to making reading difficulty Japanese text easier. But I would not recommend this for Japanese students unless you’ve had a few solid years or study, and tackled at least a few easier books.

One funny thing that happened while reading the book was when I came across a very strange piece of Japanese (nothing you would ever hear in real life), and decided to ask Claude what it meant. This was an experiment and the first time I had asked AI for the meaning of something in Japanese. Claude explained the meaning (and yes, it was definitely not normal Japanese), but as a side note made a comment about the story’s plot, throwing a big spoiler at me. This upset me and also colored my reading of the rest of the book, but it wasn’t until I finished “Novel” that I had another surprising discovery: part of the spoiler was hallucinated. In any case, while I acknowledge the value of AI in this day and age, with the current technologies asking it to explain parts of a book is very risky and not recommended!

I do want to talk briefly about one more aspect of this book: the overarching theme. Obviously it’s related to the idea of the “novel”, and the author brings together various strands to weave an interesting premise: philosophy, science (including information theory!), and the fictional (?) worlds of a few famous poets/authors.

By the end of the book, I was impressed with the author’s creativity on this front (which is perhaps why it won a literary award). But at the same time, I was nonplussed with how the author deployed his message: telling his ideas (sometimes through other character’s speech) directly through longish information-dump sessions that were clustered around a few parts of the book. I’ve written and read enough literature to know that “show not tell” is not a blanket rule that you should apply to all writing, but in this case I would have appreciated more events and actions to show his ideas instead of just saying “You see, the world is like this and novels exist to do this…”
After everything, I’m still going to give a mild recommendation for this book, since I don’t regret the read.
